blind_results.reasoning: Pregabalin is a federal Schedule V controlled substance (21 CFR 1308.15(e)(7), DEA code 2782). Massachusetts Schedule V is defined by incorporation: 105 CMR 700.002(E) provides that Schedule V 'shall consist of the drugs and other substances ... listed in 21 CFR 1308.15.' Pregabalin is therefore Massachusetts Schedule V, not Schedule VI. The controlling Massachusetts refill rule is 247 CMR 9.04(13): 'A licensee may not fill or refill a prescription for a Schedule V controlled substance more than six months after the date on which said prescription was issued. A prescription for a Schedule V controlled substance may not be refilled more than five times.' The two limits are independent and cumulative. Here only five months have elapsed, so the six-month window has not closed, but five refills have already been dispensed, so the five-refill ceiling is exhausted and no further quantity may be supplied on that prescription; new prescriber authorization is required. A is wrong because the one-year validity period belongs to Schedule VI (247 CMR 9.04(12)), not Schedule V. B is wrong because a Schedule V drug does not become Schedule VI: 105 CMR 700.002(F) confines Schedule VI to prescription drugs 'not included in any other schedule.' D is wrong because it treats the six-month window as the only operative limit and ignores the separate five-refill ceiling in the same sentence of 247 CMR 9.04(13).

blind_results.reasoning: 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) fixes the MassPAT submission stream: reporting applies to a pharmacy 'that dispenses a controlled substance pursuant to a prescription in Schedules II through V, or a controlled substance classified by the Department as an additional drug as outlined in 105 CMR 700.012.' 105 CMR 700.001 defines 'Additional Drug' as 'a controlled substance in Schedule VI determined by the Department to carry a bona fide potential for abuse,' and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(8) supplies the designation criteria. (B) Pregabalin is Massachusetts Schedule V (105 CMR 700.002(E) incorporating 21 CFR 1308.15(e)(7)), so it is reportable as a Schedule II-V prescription dispensing. (A) Gabapentin is a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug (105 CMR 700.002(F)) that the Commissioner has designated an additional drug; the Department's Drug Control Program states pharmacies 'are required to submit data to the PMP for all dispensations of Schedule II-V medications and Gabapentin, a Schedule VI medication designated by the Commissioner as a drug of concern,' citing 105 CMR 700.012(7). Gabapentin is therefore reportable on the basis of the listed drug, and the indication (postherpetic neuralgia) is irrelevant to the reporting trigger. (C) An ordinary CMEA retail sale of pseudoephedrine is a non-prescription over-the-counter transaction in a scheduled listed chemical product, not the dispensing of a Schedule II-V controlled substance or an additional drug pursuant to a prescription; it falls outside 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) and instead sits in the federal regulated-seller regime of 21 CFR part 1314. (D) is therefore false because A and B are both in-stream.

blind_results.reasoning: Methylphenidate is Schedule II (21 CFR 1308.12(d)(4), DEA code 1724; Massachusetts Schedule II by incorporation at 105 CMR 700.002(B)). M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) governs patient-requested partial filling of a Schedule II prescription and states in terms: 'The remaining portion may be filled upon patient request in accordance with federal law; provided, however, that only the same pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity shall dispense the remaining portion.' The second pharmacy therefore has no lawful route to supply the balance, regardless of how many days have elapsed. The federal window in 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) (remaining portions 'must be filled not later than 30 days after the date on which the prescription is written') and the parallel 30-day limit in s. 18(d3/4) run in the patient's favour on timing, but they do not relax the same-pharmacy restriction. A is wrong twice over: the balance of a partial fill is not a refill (Schedule II prescriptions may not be refilled, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(b)) and Schedule II prescriptions are not transferable. C is wrong because nothing converts an unfilled remainder into a new prescription at day 31; s. 23(a) makes the Schedule II prescription invalid 30 days after issuance and s. 18(d3/4) closes the remainder window at the same point. D is wrong because dispensing does not reschedule a drug; methylphenidate remains Schedule II.

blind_results.reasoning: Two distinct federal retail quantity ceilings apply to a scheduled listed chemical product. The seller-side daily ceiling is 21 CFR 1314.20(a): a regulated seller may not sell a customer more than '3.6 grams of ephedrine base, 3.6 grams of pseudoephedrine base, or 3.6 grams of phenylpropanolamine base' in a single calendar day, 'without regard to the number of transactions.' The purchaser-side 30-day ceiling is 21 U.S.C. 844(a): it is unlawful 'to knowingly or intentionally purchase at retail during a 30 day period more than 9 grams of ephedrine base, pseudoephedrine base, or phenylpropanolamine base in a scheduled listed chemical product.' A single 4.0 gram purchase exceeds 3.6 grams and so is barred by the daily ceiling. With no purchases in the preceding 30 days the running 30-day total would be 4.0 grams, well under 9 grams, so the 30-day ceiling is not reached. A inverts the two figures; C asserts both are exceeded, which is arithmetically false on the 30-day leg; D is false because the daily ceiling is exceeded. The 7.5 gram 30-day figure in 21 CFR 1314.20(b) applies only to mobile retail vendors and is not engaged by an 'ordinary retail transaction'.

blind_results.reasoning: Buprenorphine is a Schedule III narcotic (21 CFR 1308.13(e)(2)(i), DEA code 9064), and Massachusetts Schedule III is defined by incorporation of 21 CFR 1308.13 at 105 CMR 700.002(C). Combining buprenorphine with naloxone does not remove the product from Schedule III; the combination product is scheduled as such. The Massachusetts quantity framework is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(d), which caps most Schedule II or III prescriptions at a 30-day supply per filling but provides that prescriptions 'may be filled for a maximum of a 90-day supply of such substance upon a single filling for: (i) the treatment of opioid use disorder, including, but not limited to, buprenorphine.' A prescription for buprenorphine-naloxone written for opioid use disorder is squarely inside clause (i), so the drug's Schedule III status and the 90-day OUD carve-out are the correct linkage. A is wrong: adding an antagonist does not decontrol a scheduled narcotic. B is wrong on two counts: not every opioid-related product is Schedule II, and Schedule III prescriptions may carry refills subject to 21 CFR 1306.22(a). D is wrong because 105 CMR 700.002(F) limits Schedule VI to prescription drugs not included in any other schedule, and dispensing does not reschedule anything.

blind_results.reasoning: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) sets out the sequence in the order its sentences run. First, the patient's request precedes and triggers the reduced initial quantity: 'A pharmacist filling a prescription for a schedule II substance shall, if requested by the patient, dispense the prescribed substance in a lesser quantity than indicated on the prescription' (choice B). Second, that initial reduced dispensing occurs, and the statute bounds it: 'The initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to subsection (d) or (d1/2) shall be filled not more than 5 days after the prescription issue date' (choice D). Third, the patient returns for the balance, and only one pharmacy may supply it: 'The remaining portion may be filled upon patient request ... provided, however, that only the same pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity shall dispense the remaining portion' (choice A). Fourth, the completing dispensing is bounded by the outer window: 'The remaining portion filled pursuant to this subsection must be filled not later than 30 days after the prescription issue date' (choice C), which is congruent with 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) and with the 30-day validity of a Schedule II prescription under s. 23(a). The chronological order is therefore B, D, A, C.

blind_results.reasoning: Buprenorphine-naloxone is Schedule III (21 CFR 1308.13(e)(2)(i); Massachusetts Schedule III by incorporation at 105 CMR 700.002(C)). 21 CFR 1306.22(a) provides that no prescription for a controlled substance listed in Schedule III or IV shall be filled or refilled more than six months after the date on which it was issued, nor be refilled more than five times. The six-month clock runs from the issue date, not from the first dispensing, and an authorized-but-unused refill does not survive expiry of that window; a new prescription is required. B states the rule that the regulation does not adopt (measuring from first dispensing). C is wrong because the naloxone component does not alter scheduling or the refill window, and the one-year figure belongs to Massachusetts Schedule VI under 247 CMR 9.04(12). D is wrong because an unused refill authorization does not migrate to another schedule; 105 CMR 700.002(F) confines Schedule VI to prescription drugs not included in any other schedule.

blind_results.reasoning: 21 CFR 1306.22 is by its terms confined to Schedules III and IV; it supplies no refill ceiling for Schedule V, and 21 CFR 1306.23 addresses only partial filling of Schedule III, IV and V prescriptions. A pharmacist who stopped there would wrongly conclude that Schedule V refills are unconstrained. Massachusetts fills that gap independently: 247 CMR 9.04(13) provides that 'A licensee may not fill or refill a prescription for a Schedule V controlled substance more than six months after the date on which said prescription was issued. A prescription for a Schedule V controlled substance may not be refilled more than five times.' That is the reason the analysis must continue past the federal text. A is fabricated; no federal provision reschedules a Schedule V drug on dispensing. B is wrong as a matter of preemption doctrine and of the CSA's own savings provision at 21 U.S.C. 903, which leaves states free to regulate unless there is a positive conflict; Massachusetts imposing a stricter refill rule creates no such conflict. C is wrong because Schedule V substances are controlled substances by definition (21 CFR 1308.15; 105 CMR 700.002(E)) and do carry refill restrictions in Massachusetts.
